newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - Feb 20.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - Feb 20.

text.p: The following stories were reported in Thursday's electronic version of The Wall Street Journal:
* The inflation rate slowed in January, with the consumer price index rising 0.1 percent, below December's 0.3 percent rise.
* The U.S. trade deficit widened to an eight-year high of 114.23 billion in 1996.
* Goldman Sachs strategist Abby Cohen shifted her bullish stance, saying the market could be entering a trading range after topping 7,000.
* Steven Brill, the founder and chief executive of American Lawyer Media, is selling his interest in Court TV and other ventures to Time Warner for more than $20 million.
* Ford sold its heavy truck unit to Daimler-Benz's Freightliner in what some analysts believe is a deal worth about $200 million.
* Great Western, the target of a hostile bid by H.F. Ahmanson, could attract rival bids from NationsBank and Seattle's Washington Mutual.
* Cablevision said it plans to put nearly $1 billion of its cable systems up for sale and use some proceeds to pay down its $4 billion debt.
* The Dow industrials fell 47.33 to 7,020.13. Bond prices fell, and the dollar rose.
* Age-bias lawsuits are being spurned in incidents where employers' actions hurt older workers more than others but didn't involve intential bias.

* The Securities and Exchange Commission has broadened its investigation of municipal-bond "yield burning" to include a former Pennsylvania insurer, Alex. Brown and the informant who spurred the inquiry.
* Levi Strauss & Co plans to cut 20 percent of its white-collar work force because of increased competition and less demand for jeans.
* Knight-Ridder's The Detroit Free Press and Gannett's The Detroit News agreed to an offer by six striking unions for workers to return to their jobs.
* General Motors will offer 20 percent of Delphi Automotive to the public after it merges Delphi with Delco Electronics.
* Fluor's shares fell 17 percent after the construction giant posted disappointing quarterly profit because of cost overruns at two power projects.
* When the Dow Jones Industrial Average blasted through the 7,000 mark a week ago today, market strategist Abby Cohen was absent from the pundit chorus predicting Next Stop 8,000.

The next day, she faxed clients a notably unbullish warning that the market may be heading into "a trading range." And in recent weeks, she has been calling the market "mostly overvalued." -- Heard on the Street.
* What began two years ago as a routine inquiry into a seemingly obscure practice on Wall Street is now shaking the $1.3 trillion municipal-bond market.

The Securities and Exchange Commission is ratcheting up its scrutiny of municipal-bond "yield-burning" abuses. State and local governments are fretting about how much the mess could cost them, and regulators are drawing into their sights some interesting figures, including a former Pennsylvania state treasurer, an old-line brokerage firm, Alex. Brown Inc. and surprisingly, Michael Lissack, the self-styled whistle-blower who brought on the investigation in the first place, people familiar with the matter say. -- Credit Markets.
-- New York newsdesk 212-859-1610.
